text: The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin, a pilot from the Soviet Union. On 12 April 1961, he was launched in a small spacecraft called Vostok 1. He circled Earth once, travelling at about 27,000 km/h, and landed safely 108 minutes after [[@maths-countdown|lift-off]].

As the rocket roared off the pad, Gagarin called out "Poyekhali!", Russian for "Let's go!". He was 27 years old. After his flight he became one of the most famous people on Earth, and 12 April is now celebrated by the United Nations as the International Day of Human Space Flight.

He stayed inside and landed on a runway
He splashed down in the ocean

st.reveal: Vostok's capsule landed quite hard, so the plan was always for the pilot to eject at about 7 km up and parachute down separately. The Soviet Union kept this quiet for years, partly because record rules then said a pilot had to land with his craft.

sec.t:
Yuri Gagarin was born in 1934 in a village called Klushino, west of Moscow. His parents worked on a collective farm. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], German soldiers occupied his village, and his family lived for a time in a dugout in the ground.

After the war he trained as a metalworker, then joined a flying club and later the Soviet Air Force as a fighter pilot. In 1960 he was chosen as one of 20 young pilots to train as cosmonauts, the Russian word for astronauts. One reason he was picked for the first flight was practical: he was only about 1.57 m tall, which helped in the cramped capsule. He was also calm and cheerful under pressure.

Vostok 1 was launched from [[@launch-sites|Baikonur]], in what is now Kazakhstan, the same site that had sent up [[@sputnik|Sputnik]] four years earlier. The spacecraft was a ball about 2.3 m wide, with a small window. Most of the flight was controlled automatically, because nobody knew whether a human could think clearly while weightless. Gagarin had a sealed envelope with a code to switch on the manual controls in an emergency.

He looked out at Earth and reported what he saw, including the thin blue band of the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] at the edge of the planet. He said he felt well, and that weightlessness did not stop him working, writing notes or thinking clearly.

At about 7 km above the ground, he ejected from the capsule and floated down by parachute, wearing a bright orange [[@spacesuits|spacesuit]]. He landed in a field near the town of Engels, in southern [[@russia|Russia]]. A farm woman and her granddaughter were the first people to meet him. He told them not to be afraid, because he was a Soviet citizen like them.

{{story:russia}}

Gagarin's flight was a huge victory for the Soviet Union in its [[@space-race|space race]] with the United States. Less than a month later, on 5 May 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space, on a 15-minute flight that went up and came straight back down. In February 1962, John Glenn became the first American to [[orbit|orbit]] Earth.

Before people flew, both countries had [[@space-animals|sent animals]]. In August 1960 two Soviet dogs, Belka and Strelka, orbited Earth and came home safely, which helped convince engineers that a human could survive the trip.

On 16 June 1963, [[@women-in-space|Valentina Tereshkova]], a former [[textile|textile]] factory worker and keen parachutist, flew Vostok 6. She orbited Earth 48 times in nearly three days, longer than all the American astronauts up to then put together. She was 26. Nearly 20 years passed before another woman went to space.

Gagarin never flew in space again. He was too precious to risk. He toured the world, including India in 1961, where he met Prime Minister Jawaharlal [[@nehru|Nehru]]. In 1968 he died in a training jet crash, aged 34.

Less than ten years after Gagarin's 108 minutes, astronauts were walking on the Moon during [[@apollo-moon|Apollo 11]]. India plans to launch its own astronauts through its Gaganyaan programme.

text: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the second-largest moon in the [[solar-system|solar system]], after Jupiter's Ganymede. It is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

It is the only moon with a thick [[atmosphere|atmosphere]], and the only place besides Earth known to have stable liquid on its surface. But Titan is extremely cold, about −180 °C. There, methane and ethane, which are gases on Earth, form clouds, fall as rain, carve rivers and fill lakes and seas. Water is frozen solid and acts like rock.
Below its icy crust, scientists think Titan also hides an ocean of salty liquid water.

st.reveal: Dragonfly is a nuclear-powered rotorcraft with eight rotors. Titan's thick air and low gravity make flying much easier than on Earth, so it can hop from site to site, travelling kilometres at a time.

sec.t:
Titan's air is mostly nitrogen, like Earth's, but at ground level it is about four times denser than the air you breathe. The pressure at the surface is about one and a half times what you feel on Earth, similar to being a few metres underwater in a swimming pool.

Sunlight breaks up methane high in the air and builds new, more complicated chemicals. These form a thick orange [[@fog-smog|smog]] that hides the surface. When the Voyager spacecraft flew past in 1980, its cameras saw only a fuzzy orange ball.

In 2004, the Cassini spacecraft, built by NASA, the European Space Agency and Italy, arrived at Saturn. It carried a European probe named Huygens, after the Dutch [[astronomer|astronomer]] Christiaan Huygens, who discovered Titan in 1655.

On 14 January 2005, Huygens parachuted down through the haze for more than two hours. It landed on a damp plain scattered with rounded pebbles of water ice, like stones in a dry riverbed. It is still the most distant landing ever made by a spacecraft.

Cassini kept studying Titan for 13 years. Its radar could see through the haze and found lakes and seas near the north pole. The biggest, Kraken Mare, is larger than the Caspian Sea, the biggest lake on Earth.

{{story:helicopters}}

On Earth, water evaporates from the sea, forms clouds and falls as rain in the [[@water-cycle|water cycle]]. On Titan, methane does the same job. Cassini watched clouds form and saw dark patches appear after storms, where the ground had become wet.

The rain falls slowly. With low [[gravity|gravity]] and thick air, raindrops on Titan drift down at about walking speed, and they can grow larger than raindrops on Earth.

Titan's lakes hold far more methane and ethane than all of Earth's known [[@oil-coal|oil and gas]] reserves. Dunes made of dark grains of carbon-rich material wrap around its middle, like the sand seas of the Sahara.

Titan has many of the chemicals that may have come before life on Earth. Some scientists wonder whether strange forms of life could use liquid methane instead of water, though nobody knows if that is possible. The [[@space-weird-oceans-moons|hidden ocean of water]] beneath the crust is another place where [[@alien-life|life might exist]].

To find out more, NASA is building Dragonfly, a car-sized flying machine with eight [[rotor|rotors]], like a giant [[@drones|drone]]. It is planned to launch in 2028 and reach Titan in the 2030s. It will fly from place to place, landing to sniff and sample the ground, on a world where flying is easier than walking. Titan's gravity is only about a seventh of Earth's. Some scientists have worked out that, in air that thick, a person with wings strapped to their arms could flap their way off the ground, if they could survive the cold.

text: Not really. Crocodile relatives once included fast land runners and sea-going hunters. Today's crocodiles are only a few survivors.

The crocodile family tree goes back more than 200 million years, to the same early group that gave rise to dinosaurs and, later, birds. That group is called the archosaurs, or "ruling reptiles". Crocodiles look a lot like their ancestors from the [[@dino-age-span|age of dinosaurs]], so people call them [[@living-fossils|living fossils]]. But they have kept changing, and the line has been through many shapes.
India has three crocodilians: the mugger, the saltwater crocodile and the gharial.
The gharial, with its long thin snout for catching fish, is critically [[endangered|endangered]]. The Chambal river is one of its last homes.

myth: Crocodiles are living fossils that haven't changed since the time of the dinosaurs.

Today's crocodiles look ancient, but they have kept evolving. Their extinct relatives included fast runners on land, sea-going hunters with flippers, and plant-eaters. Modern crocodiles are the few survivors of a once much more varied family.

sec.t: About 66 million years ago, [[@space-asteroid-defence|an asteroid]] struck Earth and wiped out the giant dinosaurs. Many crocodile relatives died too, but some made it through. Scientists think a few habits helped them. Crocodiles are cold-blooded, so they need far less food than a warm-blooded animal of the same size and can go months without eating. Living in rivers and lakes, they could feed on fish and dead animals, which were easier to find than fresh plants after the [[@extinction|disaster]].

The mugger lives in rivers, lakes and [[reservoir|reservoirs]] across India, and even in some city ponds. The saltwater crocodile, the largest reptile alive, lives in the [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]], the [[@mangroves|mangroves]] of Bhitarkanika in Odisha and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Large males can grow longer than 6 metres.

The gharial is the odd one out. Its narrow snout is lined with small, sharp teeth, perfect for snapping up fish but no good for big prey. Adult males grow a round lump on the tip of the snout, shaped like a clay pot called a *ghara*, which gave the animal its name. They use it to make buzzing sounds and bubbles.

By the 1970s, gharials had almost vanished, with only around 200 thought to be left in the wild. India started a crocodile conservation project in 1975, collecting eggs from riverbanks and raising young gharials until they were big enough to release. Today the National Chambal Sanctuary, on a long stretch of the Chambal river, holds most of the world's wild gharials.

Crocodiles are careful parents. A mother mugger digs a nest in a sandy bank and guards it for about two months. Temperature inside the nest decides whether the babies hatch as males or females. When she hears the hatchlings squeak, she digs them out and carries them to the water in her jaws, the same jaws that can crush bone.

That kind of care is something crocodiles share with birds, their [[@birds-dinosaurs|closest living relatives]]. Both build nests, both guard their young, and both probably inherited these habits from ancestors they shared with the dinosaurs.

text: For its size, the strongest known animal may be a tiny mite that lives in soil. In a 2007 study, one held on against a pull of about 1,180 times its own body weight. Close behind is a horned dung beetle, which in a 2010 study pulled about 1,141 times its weight. For a person, that would be like dragging about 80 tonnes, as heavy as a dozen elephants.

[[@ants-world|Ants]] are famous for strength too. Asian weaver ants can cling upside down to glass while holding 100 times their own weight. But the winners change depending on whether you measure pulling, carrying, holding or biting.

options.t: It would be weak and could hardly hold itself up
It could lift a lorry over its head

st.reveal: Making an animal bigger raises its weight much faster than its muscle strength. A giant ant would be crushed by its own body and couldn't even breathe properly. Superstrength only works at a tiny size.

sec.t:
The horned dung beetle lives in tunnels under cow pats. Males fight over females in narrow underground passages, pushing and shoving with the horns on their heads. That's why they need such strength.

Scientists at the University of Western Australia tied a thread to beetles and measured how hard they could pull before being dragged out of a tube. The strongest beat 1,141 times their weight. Smaller, hornless males, which avoid fights and sneak past the big ones instead, turned out to be much weaker. [[@power-dung-beetle|Dung beetles]] have other talents too, like rolling balls of dung in straight lines by following the stars.

Ants aren't just strong, they're tough. In 2014 engineers in the USA studied a type of mound ant and found its neck joint could withstand forces of about 5,000 times its body weight before breaking.

The [[@power-mantis-shrimp|mantis shrimp]] is a champion puncher. It swings its club-like arm so fast that the water boils into tiny bubbles, which pop and hit the prey a second time. It can smash snail shells, and aquarium owners say it has cracked glass tanks.

For the strongest bite ever measured, the winner is the saltwater crocodile, whose jaws snap shut harder than any other living animal tested.

Strength isn't only about lifting. Some small animals are champions at turning muscle into sudden movement. A froghopper, an insect about 6 millimetres long, can leap around 70 centimetres into the air, more than 100 times its own length. Fleas and grasshoppers store energy in springy parts of their bodies, then release it all at once like a catapult.

In the sea, tiny crustaceans called copepods kick themselves away from danger at hundreds of body lengths a second.

These feats follow the same square-cube rule: small bodies are light, so a little muscle goes a long way. But tiny animals face a problem big ones don't. To a very small insect, air feels thick and sticky, a bit like swimming through syrup.

If you only count raw power, big animals win easily. An African elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of tiny muscle bundles and no bones. It can rip branches off trees and lift heavy logs, yet pick up a single peanut.

Humans, by the way, are quite weak for our size compared with insects or even chimpanzees. Our bodies trade raw strength for control and [[endurance|endurance]]. And the strangest part? Some ants team up and use their own bodies as building blocks, making living [[@power-ant-bridges|bridges]] for the rest of the colony to cross.

text: Your eyes are about 6 cm apart, so each one sees the world from a slightly different spot. Your brain compares the two views and uses the small differences to work out how far away things are. This is called stereo vision.

A 3D film copies this trick. It is filmed with two cameras side by side, like a pair of eyes. In the cinema, both pictures are shown on the screen at the same time, overlapping. Without glasses, they look blurry and doubled.

The glasses are filters. Each lens lets through only the picture meant for that eye and blocks the other. Your brain receives two slightly different views, combines them as it always does, and the scene appears to have depth.

st.prompt: In the middle of a 3D film, you close one eye. What happens to the picture?

options.t: It looks flat, like a normal film

st.reveal: 3D films work by giving each eye a different picture. With one eye shut, your brain gets only one picture, so the depth disappears. Your brain still uses clues like size and shadow to guess distance, but the pop-out effect is gone.

d.try: Hold one finger up about 30 cm from your face, in front of a far-off door frame. Close your left eye, then your right, and switch quickly back and forth. Your finger seems to jump sideways, because each eye sees it from a slightly different spot. That difference is what 3D films copy.
myth: Watching 3D films damages children's eyes.

Eye doctors say there's no evidence that 3D films harm healthy eyes. Some people get tired eyes or headaches, which go away when they stop. Trouble seeing 3D can be a sign of an eye problem that's worth checking with a doctor.
facts: each eye gets a slightly different picture

sec.t:
Hold up a pencil at arm's length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps against the background. Close objects jump a lot, distant ones hardly at all. Your [[@brain-works|brain]] measures those jumps, in a fraction of a second, without you noticing.

In 1838, the English scientist Charles Wheatstone built a device called a stereoscope. It used mirrors to show a different drawing to each eye, and viewers saw a single scene with depth. Within a few decades, stereoscopes with pairs of photographs became a popular entertainment in Victorian homes in Britain and America.

sec.h: Three ways to split the picture
sec.t:
The oldest kind of 3D glasses have one red lens and one blue or cyan lens. The two pictures are printed or shown in matching colours. The red lens blocks one picture, the blue lens blocks the other. They're cheap, but colours look odd.

Most cinemas now use polarised glasses. Light waves can wiggle in different directions. [[@projectors|The projector]] sends one picture with light that twists one way and the other picture twisting the opposite way, and each lens of the glasses lets only one twist through. Colours look normal.

Some 3D televisions used battery-powered shutter glasses. Each lens darkens and clears many times a second, in time with the screen flashing between left and right pictures.

{{story:vr-ar}}

3D films have come and gone in waves. Hollywood had a 3D boom in the early 1950s, when studios hoped the novelty would pull families away from their new televisions. Another big wave came in 2009, when the film Avatar became a huge hit in 3D.

In India, the first 3D feature film was *My Dear Kuttichathan*, made in [[@malayalam|Malayalam]] and released in 1984. It told the story of a friendly little spirit and the children who free him. Audiences across [[@cinema-south|South India]] lined up to wear the glasses. The film was later dubbed into Hindi and other languages and shown across the country.

sec.h: Why some people can't see it
sec.t:
Not everyone sees 3D films the same way. A small share of people have weak stereo vision, often because their eyes didn't learn to work together properly in early childhood. For them, 3D films look flat or uncomfortable.

Some people also get tired eyes or headaches. In real life, your eyes point at and focus on the same spot. In a 3D film they have to point at objects that seem to float in front of the screen while still focusing on the screen itself. Virtual reality headsets face the same puzzle. If 3D always looks wrong to you, it's worth getting your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] checked.

text: सुलेख यानी कला की तरह की गई लिखावट। इसका अंग्रेज़ी नाम कैलिग्राफ़ी यूनानी भाषा से आया है और इसका मतलब है "सुंदर लिखावट"। दुनिया के कई हिस्सों में लोगों ने अक्षरों के आकार को उतनी ही गंभीरता से लिया है, जितनी गंभीरता से चित्रकार रंगों को लेते हैं।

जगह बदलते ही औज़ार और नियम बदल जाते हैं। चीनी सुलेखक नरम ब्रश चलाते हैं। अरबी सुलेखक सरकंडे से कटी कलम। [[medieval|मध्यकाल]] के यूरोप के भिक्षु पंखों से बनी कलम इस्तेमाल करते थे। भारत में लिपिकार दर्जनों [[script|लिपियों]] में ताड़-पत्रों और कागज़ पर लिखते थे। सुलेख जहाँ भी पनपा, उसने एक काम की चीज़ को ऐसी चीज़ बना दिया जिसे लोग दीवारों पर टाँगते हैं, इमारतों में तराशते हैं और ज़िंदगी भर साधते हैं।

sec.t:
चीन में ब्रश से लिखना लगभग 2,000 साल से सबसे ऊँची कलाओं में से एक रहा है। हर [[@chinese-characters|चीनी अक्षर]] तय क्रम में खींची गई रेखाओं से बनता है, और सुलेखक हर रेखा पर काबू रखता है: मोटी लकीर के लिए दबाना, पतली पूँछ के लिए उठाना।

सबसे मशहूर सुलेखक वांग शीझी 300 के दशक में हुए। एक नदी किनारे कविता की महफ़िल में उन्होंने जो छोटा-सा टुकड़ा लिखा, वह चीनी कला की सबसे ज़्यादा नकल की गई रचना बन गया। जापान ने ब्रश से लिखना चीन से सीखा और इसे शोदो कहता है, यानी "लिखने का मार्ग"। जापानी स्कूली बच्चे आज भी इसका अभ्यास करते हैं, कागज़ की लंबी पट्टियों पर झुककर, काली स्याही से।

बच्चे आदर्श अक्षरों की बार-बार नकल करके सीखते हैं, कुछ-कुछ वैसे जैसे हमारे यहाँ सुलेख की कॉपी में बिंदुओं पर अक्षर लिखे जाते हैं। कुछ बच्चे एक ख़ास कपड़े पर सादे पानी से अभ्यास करते हैं, जो गीला होने पर गहरा हो जाता है और सूखते ही फीका पड़ जाता है, इसलिए एक ही कपड़ा बरसों चलता है। चीनी शहरों के पार्कों में बुज़ुर्ग लोग लंबे स्पंज वाले ब्रश और पानी से फ़ुटपाथ पर बड़े-बड़े अक्षर लिखते हैं। शब्द कुछ ही मिनटों में गायब हो जाते हैं, और यही इस खेल का मज़ा है।

छपाई से पहले यूरोप की हर किताब हाथ से नकल की जाती थी, अक्सर भिक्षुओं के हाथों। लगभग 800 में आयरलैंड में बनी बुक ऑफ़ केल्स के पन्ने लिपटते-मुड़ते अक्षरों, रंगे हुए जानवरों और गाँठों से भरे हैं।

भारत में लिपिकार धातु की नुकीली सुई से सूखे ताड़-पत्रों पर अक्षर खुरचते थे और फिर उन्हें गहरा करने के लिए कालिख मलते थे। ओड़िया और मलयालम जैसी गोल लिपियाँ शायद कुछ हद तक इसलिए बनीं क्योंकि पत्ते की नसों के साथ सीधी लकीर उसे चीर सकती थी। सिख लिपिकारों ने सदियों तक गुरु ग्रंथ साहिब को गुरमुखी में हाथ से उतारा, और कुछ आज भी ऐसा करते हैं।

जो अक्षर तुम रोज़ पढ़ते हो, उन्हें सुलेख ने गढ़ा है। 1916 में एडवर्ड जॉन्स्टन नाम के एक सुलेखक ने लंदन की ज़मीन के नीचे चलने वाली रेल, लंदन अंडरग्राउंड, के लिए अक्षर बनाए, जो आज भी चलते हैं। बहुत-से कंप्यूटर [[@fonts|फ़ॉन्ट]] ऐसे अक्षरों पर टिके हैं जो पहले कलम या ब्रश से बने थे।

ऐपल शुरू करने वाले स्टीव जॉब्स ने बाद में कहा कि कॉलेज में ली गई सुलेख की एक क्लास की वजह से उन्हें कंप्यूटर पर सुंदर अक्षरों की परवाह हुई। आज के कलाकार पुराने और नए को मिलाते हैं, दीवारों पर विशाल अक्षर रंगते हैं या देवनागरी को ग्रैफ़िटी के साथ घोलते हैं। भारत में दुकानों के बोर्ड, शादी के कार्ड और फ़िल्मों के पोस्टर अक्सर आज भी हाथ से बने देवनागरी, तमिल या बांग्ला अक्षरों से सजते हैं, और कई शहरों में सुलेख की क्लासें लोकप्रिय हो गई हैं। ब्रश की रेखाएँ अब भले डिजिटल हों, पर संतुलन और जगह के नियम सदियों पुराने हैं।

text: Diwali comes from the Sanskrit *deepavali*, meaning "a row of lamps". On Diwali night, families light clay lamps called [[@candles|diyas]] in rows along doorsteps, windows and rooftops. It falls on the new moon of the month of Kartik, the darkest night, so the lamps shine brightest.
The lights stand for light winning over darkness and good over evil. Homes are cleaned and decorated, people wear new clothes, [[@sharing-science|share sweets]] and visit friends and relatives.
Because it follows the [[@moon-phases|Moon]], Diwali moves around the calendar, usually landing in October or November.

Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas at the same time, Jains mark the day Mahavira attained nirvana, and some Buddhists, especially Newars in Nepal, celebrate too. Each has its own reasons for lighting lamps.

sec.t:
For many Hindus, Diwali marks the return of Lord Rama to Ayodhya after 14 years in exile, as told in the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]]. People lit lamps to welcome him home. Many also worship the goddess Lakshmi, who is linked with wealth and good fortune.

In parts of South India, the main day celebrates Krishna's victory over the demon Narakasura. In Bengal, the same night is Kali Puja. Sikhs celebrate *Bandi Chhor Divas*, remembering Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior Fort, and the Golden Temple in Amritsar glows with lights. Jains remember [[@mahavira|Mahavira]], who attained nirvana, or final release, on this night.

In much of north and west India, Diwali stretches over five days. It starts with Dhanteras, when many families buy something new, often metal pots or gold. Next comes Naraka Chaturdashi, sometimes called Choti Diwali.

The third day is the main festival, with Lakshmi Puja and the lamps. Then comes Govardhan Puja, and in some regions a [[@new-year|new year]] begins. The last day, Bhai Dooj, celebrates brothers and sisters. Traditions differ from region to region, which is part of the fun.

Families draw rangoli or [[@rangoli-symmetry|kolam]] patterns with coloured powder, rice flour or flower petals to welcome guests. Many designs are symmetrical and built from dots and loops. Strings of marigolds and mango leaves hang over doors.

Kitchens are busy for days, making sweets like [[@food-laddoo|laddoos]], karanji and barfi to share with neighbours.

Many families also play cards or [[@board-games|board games]] on Diwali night, an old custom said to bring luck. Shops and businesses close their old account books and open new ones, which is why traders in Gujarat often treat Diwali as the start of a fresh year.

{{story:fireworks}}

Firework colours come from metals heated until they glow. Each metal gives off its own colour of light, so firework makers mix different compounds to paint the sky. Most of India's fireworks are made in [[@made-matchsticks|Sivakasi]], in Tamil Nadu.

[[@fireworks|Fireworks]] also cause air and noise pollution, and they frighten pets and birds. In northern cities, Diwali often comes as the winter air is already smoggy, so smoke from crackers adds to the problem. Courts and city governments have restricted fireworks in some years, and many families now celebrate mostly with lamps and electric lights.

Today Diwali is celebrated across India and by communities around the world, from Singapore to New York. It is a public holiday in countries such as Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Fiji and Trinidad and Tobago. In 2023, New York made Diwali a holiday for New York City's public schools, and they closed for it for the first time in 2024. Wherever it is held, the first lamp is usually lit just after sunset, as the moonless night begins.

text: Some manners are shared by almost everyone. Most people like to be greeted, thanked and offered food when they visit. But the details of how to do those things change from place to place, sometimes in opposite directions.

Slurping noodles, eating with your hand, leaving food on your plate, tipping a waiter, keeping your shoes on indoors: each of these is polite somewhere and rude somewhere else. Manners are a kind of local language. They tell people, without words, that you respect them. Like any language, they have to be learned, and nobody is born knowing the rules.

st.prompt: In Japan, why is it rude to leave your chopsticks standing upright in a bowl of rice?

options.t: It looks like a ritual done at funerals
It means you want a second helping
It is seen as a challenge to a fight

st.reveal: At Japanese Buddhist funerals, a bowl of rice with chopsticks standing in it is offered to the person who has died. Seeing it at a dinner table brings that picture to mind. In China, the upright sticks look like incense sticks used to remember the dead.

myth: Eating with your hands is messy and bad manners.

In much of India, Sri Lanka, Ethiopia and the Middle East, eating with your hand is the proper way, with careful rules of its own. You usually use only the right hand, keep the food to your fingertips and wash before and after.

sec.t:
Across much of India, eating with your right hand is normal, even at weddings and fancy dinners. People mix rice and dal with their fingertips and lift it neatly to the mouth. The left hand stays out of the food. In Ethiopia, diners tear pieces of spongy injera bread and use them to scoop up stews.

In Japan, China and Korea, chopsticks have their own rules. Don't point with them. Don't pass food from one pair to another. Never stand them upright in a bowl of rice, because that looks like a funeral offering.

In much of the USA and Europe, forks and knives rule. Even there, habits differ. Many Americans cut their food, put the knife down and switch the fork to the right hand. Many Europeans keep the fork in the left hand throughout.

Greetings vary hugely. Indians often say namaste with palms pressed together, and many touch an elder's feet for a blessing. In Japan, people bow, more deeply for someone important. In France, friends often kiss each other lightly on both cheeks. In [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]], a traditional Māori greeting called the hongi involves pressing noses and foreheads, sharing a breath. Visitors to a Māori meeting ground may be welcomed this way.

Feet carry strong meanings in parts of Asia. In India, if you accidentally touch a book or a person with your foot, you may touch them with your hand and then touch your own eyes or forehead as an apology. In Thailand, pointing your feet at someone or at a Buddha image is very rude.

Tipping confuses travellers. In the USA, restaurant staff often depend on tips, and diners usually add 15–20% to the bill. In Japan, tips are rare, and staff may chase you down the street to return money you "forgot". India falls somewhere in between. In Britain, people are known for queueing patiently, and pushing in is frowned on almost everywhere.

Ideas about time differ as well. A meeting at 10 means 10 sharp in some offices and "around 10" in others. A party invitation for 7 might mean guests arrive at 8. When people travel, these small differences cause most of the awkward moments. Asking someone "What's the custom here?" is nearly always welcome, and it's a habit that [[@cultures-respect|respecting other cultures]] depends on. Even a simple [[@thali|thali]] meal has its own order and rules, and every family seems to know a slightly different version.

text: महान पिरामिड लगभग 4,500 साल पहले फ़राओ ख़ूफ़ू के लिए उनकी क़ब्र के रूप में बनाया गया था। मज़दूरों ने चूना-पत्थर के टुकड़े काटे, उन्हें लकड़ी की स्लेज पर रखकर घसीटा, और ढलान वाले रास्तों से ऊपर खींचा।

[[archaeologist|पुरातत्वविदों]] को पास ही पिरामिड बनाने वालों का शहर मिला, जिसमें बेकरियाँ और क़ब्रें थीं। ये मिस्र के मज़दूरों की व्यवस्थित टोलियाँ थीं, न कि ग़ुलाम, जैसा पुराने किस्से कहते थे। एक समय में इस पर कितने लोग काम करते थे, इसके अनुमान लगभग 10,000 से 30,000 तक हैं। इसे बनने में लगभग 20 साल लगे।
महान पिरामिड प्राचीन दुनिया के [[@seven-wonders|सात अजूबों]] में सबसे पुराना है, और इकलौता जो आज भी खड़ा है।

[[@egypt-nile|नील नदी]] के किनारे, [[@world-cairo|आज के काहिरा]] की सीमा पर बसे गीज़ा में तीन बड़े पिरामिड हैं। सबसे बड़ा ख़ूफ़ू का है। दूसरा उनके बेटे ख़ाफ़्रे का है, और सबसे छोटा मेनकाउरे का। पास ही [[@mystery-sphinx-nose|महान स्फ़िंक्स]] दुबककर बैठा है, इंसान के सिर वाला एक शेर, जिसे ज़मीन की चट्टान को तराशकर बनाया गया।

फ़राओ को परलोक के लिए ख़ज़ाने और ज़रूरी सामान के साथ दफ़नाया जाता था, और उनके शरीर को [[@mummies|ममी]] बनाकर सुरक्षित रखा जाता था। चोरों ने बहुत पहले ही पिरामिडों में सेंध लगा दी थी, इसलिए ज़्यादातर ख़ज़ाना ग़ायब हो चुका है।

2013 में लाल सागर के एक बंदरगाह वादी अल-जर्फ़ में पुरातत्वविदों को अब तक मिले सबसे पुराने लिखे हुए [[manuscript|पपाइरस]] के पुलिंदे मिले। इनमें से कुछ मेरेर नाम के एक अधिकारी का रोज़नामचा थे।

मेरेर लगभग 40 आदमियों की एक टोली का मुखिया था। उसके नोट्स में लिखा है कि कैसे वे तूरा की खदानों से बढ़िया सफ़ेद चूना-पत्थर नावों में भरकर नील नदी और नहरों के रास्ते गीज़ा तक ख़ूफ़ू के पिरामिड के लिए ले जाते थे। इसे पढ़ना 4,500 साल पुरानी किसी निर्माण-स्थल की डायरी पढ़ने जैसा है।

महान पिरामिड लगभग 146 मीटर ऊँचा था। लगभग 3,800 साल तक यह इंसानों की बनाई सबसे ऊँची इमारत रहा, जब तक 1300 के दशक में इंग्लैंड के एक गिरजाघर की मीनार इससे आगे नहीं निकल गई। कभी इसके पत्थरों पर चिकने, चमकते सफ़ेद चूना-पत्थर की परत चढ़ी थी। यह परत ज़्यादातर बाद में दूसरी इमारतों के लिए उखाड़ ली गई, और इसकी चोटी भी ग़ायब है। इसलिए आज यह लगभग 138 मीटर ऊँचा है।

इसकी भुजाएँ लगभग ठीक-ठीक उत्तर, दक्षिण, पूरब और पश्चिम की सीध में हैं। मिस्र के लोगों ने असली उत्तर दिशा ढूँढने के लिए शायद तारों का सहारा लिया।

सबसे ऊँचे टुकड़े ऊपर कैसे पहुँचाए गए, यह ठीक-ठीक कोई नहीं जानता। कुछ विशेषज्ञ एक लंबी सीधी ढलान की बात कहते हैं। कुछ मानते हैं कि ढलान एक भुजा पर टेढ़ी-मेढ़ी ऊपर चढ़ती थी, या पिरामिड के चारों ओर लिपटी थी। एक वास्तुकार ने तो अंदर छिपी ढलान की दलील दी है। 2018 में एक प्राचीन खदान में रस्सियों के लिए खूँटों के छेद वाली एक खड़ी ढलान मिली, जो मिस्र के लोगों का एक तरीका दिखाती है।

लगभग उसी समय [[@indus-cities|सिंधु घाटी]] के महान शहरों में सीधी गलियाँ और ढकी हुई नालियाँ थीं। और दूर उत्तर में आर्कटिक के एक सुनसान द्वीप पर [[@mammoths|ऊनी मैमथ]] अब भी रहते थे। उनमें से आख़िरी मैमथ वहाँ लगभग 4,000 साल पहले तक ज़िंदा रहे।

text: Countries trade because no country can make everything it needs well and cheaply. India grows tea, writes software and makes medicines, but it does not have enough oil. Saudi Arabia has plenty of oil but little farmland. By trading, each gets things it could not easily make at home.

Trade also lets countries focus on what they do best. If one country is very good at making cars and another at growing coffee, both can end up with more cars and more coffee by specialising and swapping. That idea is called comparative advantage, and it is one of the oldest in economics.

sec.t:
In 1817, the British economist David Ricardo used a famous example. England and Portugal could both make cloth and wine. Ricardo showed that even if Portugal were better at making both, each country gained by doing more of what it did relatively best and trading for the rest.

Think of a cricket team. Your best batter might also be a decent bowler, but the team does better if she concentrates on batting and leaves bowling to others. Countries are similar.

Until the 1950s, ships were loaded by hand, sack by sack and crate by crate. It took days and cost a lot. In 1956, the American businessman Malcom McLean sent a ship called the *Ideal X* from New Jersey to Texas carrying 58 truck-sized metal boxes. Containers could be lifted straight from ship to lorry to train.

Standard containers cut the cost of shipping dramatically. Today, [[@ships-tech|giant container ships]], some longer than three football fields, carry most of the world's manufactured goods, and about 80% of world trade by volume moves by sea. A phone you buy may contain parts from a dozen countries before it is put together.

India [[export|exports]] software and IT services, medicines, refined fuels, jewellery, rice and [[textile|textiles]]. India makes a large share of the world's generic medicines, and is sometimes called a "pharmacy of the world". It imports crude oil, gold, electronics and machinery. The United States is one of India's biggest trading partners, buying Indian software services and medicines and selling aircraft, machinery and energy.

The World Trade Organization, set up in 1995, writes rules for trade between its members and settles disputes. Countries still argue constantly. Some put taxes called [[tariff|tariffs]] on [[import|imports]] to protect their own farmers or factories. Supporters say tariffs save jobs. Critics say they raise prices for everyone and invite other countries to hit back.

Most economists think open trade has helped lift hundreds of millions of people out of poverty. They also recognise that when cheap imports arrive, some factory towns lose jobs, and those people need help to find new work. How to balance these is one of the oldest debates in politics, and one that [[@shops-markets|markets]] alone do not settle.

text: A board game is a set of rules, pieces and a board that together create a challenge. A designer's job is to make that challenge fun. They decide what players are trying to do, what choices they get on each turn, how much luck is involved and how the game ends.

Most designers start with either a theme, such as building a city or racing to a temple, or a mechanic, such as rolling dice, trading cards or placing tiles. They make a rough version from paper and cardboard and test it with friends again and again. A finished game may have been played hundreds of times before anyone buys it.

sec.t:
In 1903, an American woman named Lizzie Magie designed The Landlord's Game. Players moved around a square board buying property and charging rent. She wanted to show how renting land let a few owners grow rich while everyone else grew poor. She even included a second set of rules where wealth was shared.

People made their own boards and changed the rules. One version reached a man named Charles Darrow, who sold it to the company Parker Brothers as Monopoly in 1935. It became one of the best-selling games ever, and for decades Magie's part was nearly forgotten.

Every game sits somewhere between pure luck and pure skill. Snakes and ladders is all luck: you never make a choice. [[@chess-india|Chess]] has no luck at all. Most modern games mix the two, so that beginners have a chance but good players usually win.

Designers spend a lot of time on balance. If one strategy always wins, players stop exploring. Some games add a catch-up rule that helps whoever is behind, so nobody gives up halfway. Understanding [[@probability|probability]] helps here. A designer must know that rolling a seven with two dice happens far more often than rolling a twelve.

sec.h: The settlers of a new style
sec.t:
In 1995, Klaus Teuber, a German dental technician who designed games in his spare time, released *The Settlers of Catan*, now simply called *Catan*. Players collect wood, brick and wheat, trade with each other and build roads and towns on an island made of hexagon tiles.

*Catan* had no player knocked out early, a board that changed every game and a lot of talking and trading. It sold tens of millions of copies and helped start a boom in modern board games. Germany even has a famous yearly prize for the best new game, the Spiel des Jahres, which began in 1979.

Designers watch people play their games without explaining anything. Do players understand what to do? Do they look bored while waiting for their turn? Does the game drag on too long?

Many designers say the hardest part is the rulebook. Rules must be short, clear and impossible to misread, because the designer won't be in the room when you open the box. In the end, a good game is a conversation between a designer and players they will never meet.

text: Table tennis is one of the fastest ball games there is, not because the ball flies furthest, but because the distances are so short. A top player's smash can travel at more than 100 km/h. At that speed it crosses the 2.74 m table in about a tenth of a second.

That's quicker than most people can even react. So elite players don't just react. They read their opponent's body, bat angle and swing, and guess where the ball is going before it's struck. Add heavy spin that makes the ball curve, dip and kick sideways, and you get a game where points can be won and lost in under a second.

myth: Table tennis is a gentle game that doesn't take much fitness.

At the top level, players make hundreds of quick sideways moves, lunges and explosive strokes in a match. They train strength, speed and stamina like other athletes, and their reactions are among the fastest in sport.

sec.t:
Table tennis bats are covered with sticky rubber over a thin layer of sponge. When a player brushes the ball instead of hitting it flat, the rubber grips and sets the ball spinning, often dozens of times a second.

Spin changes everything. Topspin, where the top of the ball rolls forward, makes it dive down onto the table and leap forward off it. Backspin makes it float, then check and drop. Sidespin curves it through the air. The ball's spin also makes it jump off the opponent's bat in an unexpected direction. That's why players learn to read the brush of the bat, not just watch the ball. Grip and [[@friction|friction]] between ball and rubber are what make all of this possible.

sec.h: From dinner tables to the Olympics
sec.t:
The game began in England in the 1880s as an after-dinner game. Families used books as a net, a cork or rubber ball, and sometimes the lids of cigar boxes as bats. A company named it "Ping-Pong", after the sound, and the name stuck in many countries.

Celluloid balls arrived around 1900, and rubber-covered bats soon after. Since 2014, balls have been made of a different plastic, which is slightly slower. Table tennis became an Olympic sport in 1988, and China has dominated it, winning all five gold medals at the 2024 Paris Games.

sec.h: A bus ride that changed history
sec.t:
In 1971, during the [[@cold-war|Cold War]], the USA and China had not had friendly contact for over 20 years. At the World Championships in Nagoya, Japan, American player Glenn Cowan missed his team bus and climbed onto the Chinese team's bus instead. China's star, Zhuang Zedong, chatted with him and gave him a silk picture as a gift.

Within days, China invited the US team to visit. It was a small, careful signal. In 1972, President Richard Nixon flew to Beijing, opening a new chapter between the two countries. People still call it ping-pong diplomacy.

India has a long history in the sport, especially in Bengal and Tamil Nadu. Achanta Sharath Kamal won many [[@commonwealth-games|Commonwealth Games]] medals over two decades, and Manika Batra won women's singles gold at the 2018 Commonwealth Games. In 2024, India's women's team reached the Olympic quarter-finals for the first time. As with [[@badminton-india|badminton]], a cheap table and two bats in a school or club hall are enough to start.

sec.t:
Swift was born in 1989 in Pennsylvania and grew up on a Christmas tree farm. She loved [[@country-music|country music]], the storytelling style made famous in Nashville, Tennessee. When she was about 14, her family moved near Nashville so she could pursue music.

She signed a deal as a songwriter while still in school, and released her first album in 2006, at 16. Many of the songs came from her own diary, about high school and boys she liked.

Most country singers stay country. Swift slowly mixed in pop, and with her 2014 album 1989 she switched to pop completely. In 2020, during the COVID-19 lockdowns, she surprised fans with two quiet, folk-style albums made largely by sending files back and forth with other musicians.

She has won the [[@music-awards|Grammy]] for Album of the Year four times, more than any other artist.

Many of her songs work like short stories or [[@poetry|poems]]. She names exact things: a scarf left at a sister's house, a car ride, a particular colour. Listeners fill in the rest with their own memories.

Her fans, called Swifties, love searching for hidden meanings. She puts secret messages in album notes, numbers in videos, and dates in songs. Finding them has become a game that keeps fans talking for months.

When a musician records a song, the recording itself, called the master, is usually owned by the record company. In 2019, the masters of Swift's first six albums were sold to someone she didn't want to own them.

Her answer was unusual. She recorded those albums again, note for note, and released them as "Taylor's Version". Many fans and radio stations switched to the new versions. In 2025 she bought the original masters back. Her fight made many young musicians think harder about who owns their work.

Not everyone is a fan. Some critics find her music too polished. Others have criticised her heavy use of private jets, which release a lot of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Her team has said she buys carbon credits to make up for the flights, and the debate continues.

She has never toured India, but her songs are among the most streamed in the country, and fan groups in Indian cities hold listening parties when a new album comes out. Like many stars of the [[@streaming|streaming]] era, she reaches fans in places she has never visited.

text: तुम्हारे [[@ears-hear|कान]] अपनी हिफ़ाज़त के लिए मैल बनाते हैं। बाहरी कान से कान के पर्दे तक जाने वाली पतली सुरंग को कान की नली कहते हैं, और इसकी दीवारों पर बहुत नाज़ुक त्वचा होती है। कान का मैल उस त्वचा पर परत चढ़ाकर उसे सूखने और फटने से बचाता है।

मैल चिपचिपा होता है, इसलिए धूल, बारीक कंकड़ और छोटे-मोटे कीड़े तक कान के पर्दे के पास पहुँचने से पहले ही उसमें फँस जाते हैं। यह हल्का [[acid|अम्लीय]] भी होता है, और इसमें ऐसी चीज़ें होती हैं जो बैक्टीरिया और [[fungus|फफूँद]] को पनपने से रोकती हैं। डॉक्टर इसे सेरुमेन कहते हैं।

सबसे बढ़िया बात यह कि कान अपनी सफ़ाई खुद करता है। पुराना मैल धीरे-धीरे अपने आप नली से बाहर आकर गिर जाता है, अक्सर तुम्हें पता भी नहीं चलता। कुछ लोगों में मैल ज़्यादा बनता है, और यह भी बिल्कुल आम बात है।

कान का मैल एक आम, सेहतमंद परत है जो कान की रक्षा करती है। ईयरबड अक्सर मैल को और अंदर धकेल देते हैं, नली को खरोंच सकते हैं, यहाँ तक कि कान के पर्दे को भी चोट पहुँचा सकते हैं। ज़्यादातर लोगों के लिए बाहरी कान धो लेना काफ़ी है। अगर कान बंद-से लगें, तो डॉक्टर मदद कर सकते हैं।
facts: कान की नली के बाहरी एक-तिहाई हिस्से में

sec.t:
कान का मैल एक मिश्रण है। कान की नली के बाहरी एक-तिहाई हिस्से में मौजूद [[gland|ग्रंथियाँ]] तैलीय और मोम जैसी चीज़ें बनाती हैं। ये मरी हुई त्वचा की कोशिकाओं और कुछ बालों के साथ मिल जाती हैं। नतीजा हल्का पीला, नारंगी, भूरा या धूसर कुछ भी हो सकता है।

नली के अंदरूनी हिस्से में, कान के पर्दे के पास, मैल बनाने वाली कोई ग्रंथि होती ही नहीं। इसलिए अगर बहुत अंदर मैल मिले, तो आम तौर पर उसे किसी चीज़ ने वहाँ धकेला होता है, अक्सर ईयरबड ने।

कान की नली की त्वचा एक अनोखा काम करती है। वह जहाँ है वहीं झड़ने के बजाय, कान के पर्दे से बाहर की ओर धीरे-धीरे बढ़ती है, लगभग उतनी रफ़्तार से जितनी रफ़्तार से तुम्हारे नाखून बढ़ते हैं।

बढ़ते हुए वह पुराने मैल को किसी धीमी कन्वेयर बेल्ट की तरह साथ ले चलती है। खाना चबाते और बात करते समय जबड़े के हिलने से भी मैल खिसकता है। बाहरी कान तक पहुँचते-पहुँचते मैल सूख चुका होता है और नहाते समय धुलने को तैयार रहता है।

इसीलिए ज़्यादातर लोगों को कान के अंदर सफ़ाई की कभी ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती। कुछ लोगों में, खासकर बुज़ुर्गों में या कान की मशीन लगाने वालों में, मैल जमकर कान बंद कर सकता है। तब डॉक्टर या नर्स दवा की बूँदों से उसे नरम कर सकते हैं या हल्के से धोकर निकाल सकते हैं।

sec.h: गीला या सूखा? जीन तय करते हैं
sec.t:
कान का मैल मुख्य रूप से दो तरह का होता है। गीला मैल चिपचिपा और शहद जैसा भूरा होता है। सूखा मैल भुरभुरा और धूसर होता है। 2006 में जापानी वैज्ञानिकों ने पाया कि मैल की किस्म मुख्य रूप से एक जीन पर टिकी है, जिसका नाम ABCC11 है।

तुम्हारे कान में कौन-सी किस्म है, यह अक्सर इस बात की झलक देता है कि तुम्हारे [[ancestor|पूर्वज]] कहाँ रहते थे। अफ़्रीका या यूरोप से जड़ें रखने वाले ज़्यादातर लोगों में गीला मैल होता है। सूखा मैल पूर्वी एशिया में, कोरिया, चीन और जापान जैसी जगहों पर, कहीं ज़्यादा मिलता है। भारत में दोनों किस्में मिलती हैं।

यही जीन पसीने की कुछ ग्रंथियों पर भी असर डालता है, इसलिए सूखे मैल वाले लोगों की बगलों से आम तौर पर कम बदबू आती है। तुम्हारे [[@genes-family|जीन]] में एक छोटा-सा बदलाव दो बिल्कुल अलग जगहों पर दिखाई देता है।

{{story:blue-whale}}

कान का मैल वैज्ञानिकों को जानवरों की कहानियाँ भी सुनाता है। बड़ी व्हेलों के कान की नली में पूरी ज़िंदगी परत-दर-परत मैल जमता रहता है, कुछ-कुछ पेड़ के तने के छल्लों की तरह। जब कोई व्हेल मरकर किनारे आ लगती है, तो शोधकर्ता मैल का वह ठोस डाट काटकर उसकी परतें गिन सकते हैं।

2013 में वैज्ञानिकों ने एक [[@blue-whale|ब्लू व्हेल]] के लगभग 25 सेंटीमीटर लंबे मैल के डाट में उसकी पूरी ज़िंदगी का हिसाब पढ़ लिया। परतों ने साल-दर-साल बताया कि वह कब बड़ी हुई, कितने तनाव में रही और कौन-कौन से प्रदूषक निगलती रही।

दुनिया भर के डॉक्टर एक ही सीधी सलाह देते हैं: कान में अपनी कोहनी से छोटी कोई चीज़ मत डालो। यह पुराना मज़ाक है, पर बात पते की है। इसमें ईयरबड, बालों की पिन, चाबी और माचिस की तीली सब आते हैं।

"ईयर कैंडलिंग", जिसमें कान में एक खोखली मोमबत्ती जलाई जाती है, मैल नहीं निकालती और चेहरा व कान जला सकती है। अगर कान में दर्द हो, कान बंद-सा लगे या अचानक ठीक से सुनाई देना बंद हो जाए, तो किसी बड़े को बताओ और डॉक्टर को दिखाओ।

text: बलगम तुम्हारी नाक का गंदगी पकड़ने वाला जाल है। इसका असली नाम [[mucus|म्यूकस]] है, एक फिसलन भरी, चिपचिपी परत जो नाक के अंदर बिछी रहती है। हर साँस के साथ धूल, [[pollen|परागकण]], धुआँ और कीटाणु आते हैं। म्यूकस इन्हें फेफड़ों तक पहुँचने से पहले ही पकड़ लेता है।

यह एक और काम भी करता है। नाक में आने वाली हवा ठंडी और सूखी हो सकती है, जबकि फेफड़ों को गर्म और नम हवा पसंद है। म्यूकस हर साँस को अंदर जाते हुए नम करने में मदद करता है। तुम्हारा शरीर रोज़ बलगम बनाता है, तब भी जब तुम बिल्कुल ठीक हो। पता तभी चलता है जब यह ज़्यादा हो, जैसे [[@cold-flu|ज़ुकाम]] में।

नाक के अंदर सूक्ष्म रोएँ होते हैं, जिन्हें [[cilia|सिलिया]] कहते हैं। ये हर सेकंड कई बार एक लय में आगे-पीछे हिलते हैं, जैसे क्रिकेट स्टेडियम में दर्शक लहर बनाते हैं। मिलकर ये म्यूकस की परत को धीरे-धीरे पीछे गले की ओर धकेलते हैं।

वहाँ तुम इसे निगल लेते हो, आम तौर पर बिना ध्यान दिए। सुनने में घिनौना लगता है, पर है बड़ी चतुराई की बात। तुम्हारा पेट तेज़ अम्ल से भरा है, जो म्यूकस में फँसे ज़्यादातर कीटाणुओं को खत्म कर देता है। नाक की पूरी परत लगभग हर 10 से 20 मिनट में बदल जाती है।

नाक की सूखी पपड़ी बस नथुनों के पास का म्यूकस है जो सिलिया के खिसकाने से पहले ही सूख गया, और फँसी धूल से भरा है।

sec.h: रंग और बहाव क्यों बदलता है
sec.t:
जब कीटाणु अंदर घुसते हैं, तो शरीर उन्हें बहा निकालने के लिए ज़्यादा म्यूकस भेजता है। इसीलिए ज़ुकाम में नाक बहती है। लड़ने के लिए सफ़ेद रक्त कोशिकाएँ पहुँचती हैं, और उनमें हरी रंगत वाला एक रसायन होता है, जो म्यूकस को पीला या हरा कर सकता है। यह शरीर के काम करने की निशानी है, किसी खतरनाक संक्रमण का सबूत नहीं।

ठंडे मौसम में ठीक होने पर भी नाक टपक सकती है। नाक जमा देने वाली ठंडी हवा में नमी जोड़ती है, और उस पानी का कुछ हिस्सा नाक की नोक पर जमकर बूँद बन जाता है, जैसे ठंडे गिलास पर बूँदें। तीखा खाना और रोना भी नाक बहाते हैं।

लगभग हर कोई कभी न कभी नाक कुरेदता है। यह खतरनाक नहीं, पर उँगलियाँ कीटाणुओं को नाक में ले जाती और बाहर लाती हैं, और कुरेदने से नाज़ुक अंदरूनी परत छिल सकती है और नकसीर फूट सकती है। एक-एक नथुने से हल्के से टिशू में नाक छिनकना और फिर हाथ धो लेना ज़्यादा साफ़ तरीका है।

कुछ लोग दावा करते हैं कि नाक की पपड़ी खाने से प्रतिरक्षा तंत्र को अभ्यास मिलता है, पर इसका कोई ठोस सबूत नहीं है। वैज्ञानिक इतना ज़रूर जानते हैं कि बलगम हर समय बनता रहता है। जब तुम बिल्कुल ठीक महसूस कर रहे हो, तब भी इसे पढ़ते-पढ़ते एक ताज़ा परत गले की ओर फिसल रही है।

शरीर दूसरी जगहों पर भी म्यूकस बनाता है। यह फेफड़ों, पेट और आँतों में बिछा रहता है, जहाँ एक मोटी परत तुम्हारे अपने पेट के अम्ल को तुम्हें ही पचाने से रोकती है। बहुत-से जानवर भी चिपचिपे लेस पर टिके हैं। घोंघे इसी के कालीन पर फिसलते हैं।

अगर कभी नाक बहुत दिनों तक बहती रहे, बुखार हो, या आँखों और गालों के आसपास दर्द हो, तो माँ-बाप को बताओ या डॉक्टर को दिखाओ। और सबसे अजीब बात? कुत्ते की नाक कुछ हद तक म्यूकस की वजह से गीली रहती है, जो गंध के कण पकड़ता है। इसी से कुत्तों की सूँघने की ताकत हमसे हज़ारों गुना बेहतर है, जैसा तुम [[@power-dogs-nose|कुत्ते की नाक]] वाली कहानी में पढ़ोगे।

text: An exoskeleton is a skeleton on the outside of a body. Beetles, ants, spiders and [[@crabs|crabs]] all have one. Instead of bones inside and soft skin outside, they have a tough outer shell that holds them up, protects them and gives their [[@muscles|muscles]] something to pull on.

Engineers have borrowed the idea. A robotic exoskeleton is a frame that a person straps on over their clothes, usually around the legs, hips or back. Motors, springs and sensors help the person move. Some help people who are paralysed to stand and take steps. Others help factory workers lift heavy things or hold their arms up for hours without getting tired or injured.

st.reveal: Animals with exoskeletons moult. They split the old casing, wriggle out, swell up while the new one is still soft, and wait for it to harden. Engineers face the opposite problem, since a robot suit has to fit people of different sizes.

sec.t:
The idea of a strength suit is old. In the 1960s, General Electric in the USA built Hardiman, a huge powered frame meant to let one person lift around 680 kg. The suit itself weighed about as much, and it jerked about dangerously. Only one arm ever worked properly.

Modern suits are smaller and smarter. Each has [[sensor|sensors]] that feel how the wearer is leaning or which muscles are starting to move. A small computer decides what the person is trying to do, and electric motors at the hips and knees help do it. Batteries in a backpack keep everything running.

In 2014, the US Food and Drug Administration allowed a suit called ReWalk to be used at home by people with certain spinal cord injuries. With crutches for balance, a user can stand up, walk and even climb a few stairs.

sec.h: A kick at the World Cup
sec.t:
Also in 2014, the football World Cup in Brazil opened with an unusual moment. Juliano Pinto, a young man paralysed from the chest down, wore an exoskeleton and kicked a ball on the pitch in São Paulo. Scientists from the Walk Again Project had designed the suit to respond to signals from his brain, picked up by a cap of sensors.

The kick lasted only seconds, and TV cameras barely showed it. Still, it pointed to a future where machines could read what a person intends and help their body follow. Researchers continue to test similar ideas in hospitals today.

Some of the most common exoskeletons have no motors at all. In car factories, workers who spend all day fitting parts above their heads wear vests with springs that hold up their arms. These passive suits don't make anyone stronger. They take some of the load off shoulders and backs, which can mean fewer injuries.

Armies have tested suits that help soldiers carry heavy packs over long distances. Hospitals use fixed exoskeletons on treadmills to help stroke patients relearn walking. Together with [[@prosthetics|prosthetic limbs]] and other [[@robots|robots]] that help the body, they are changing what people with injuries can do.

The biggest problems now are cost, weight and battery life. A good medical suit can cost as much as a car. Engineers are working to make them lighter, cheaper and simple enough to put on without help.

text: An ordinary computer stores information as bits, each one either 0 or 1, as in [[@binary-code|binary code]]. A quantum computer uses qubits. Thanks to the rules of quantum physics, which govern [[atom|atoms]] and tiny particles, a qubit can be in a blend of 0 and 1 at once until it is measured. This blend is called superposition.

Qubits can also be linked, so that measuring one tells you something about another, even far away. This is called entanglement. By carefully steering many qubits together, a quantum computer can solve some special problems far faster than any ordinary machine. For most everyday jobs, though, it would be no better than a laptop.

st.reveal: Quantum computers are good at special tasks, such as simulating molecules or certain kinds of code-breaking. For email, games and videos, ordinary chips are faster and far cheaper. They are likely to stay in labs and data centres.

d.try: Spin a coin on a table. While it spins, is it heads or tails? Neither yet, until it falls. That's a rough picture of a qubit in superposition. Now try spinning two coins at once and see that they land independently, unlike entangled qubits, whose results are linked.
myth: A quantum computer works by trying every possible answer at the same time and picking the right one.

It's cleverer and harder than that. A quantum computer arranges its qubits so the wrong answers cancel each other out and the right ones grow stronger, a bit like waves. Only some problems can be set up this way.

sec.t:
Qubits are fragile. A little heat, a stray [[vibration|vibration]] or a passing radio wave can knock them out of superposition, and the calculation falls apart. This loss is called decoherence.

So the most common kind, made from superconducting [[circuit|circuits]], sits inside a tall gold-coloured fridge that looks like a chandelier. It cools the chip to about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, the [[@temperature-scales|coldest possible temperature]]. That's colder than outer space, which is about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero. Other designs use trapped atoms held by [[@lasers|lasers]], or particles of light.

**Simulating nature.** Molecules follow quantum rules, so a quantum computer could model them naturally. That might help design [[@medicine-how|new medicines]], [[fertiliser|fertilisers]] and better [[@batteries|batteries]].

**[[@cryptography-maths|Breaking codes]].** In 1994 the mathematician Peter Shor showed that a big enough quantum computer could crack some of the codes that protect online banking and messages. Today's machines are far too small to do this. But governments are already switching to new kinds of [[@encryption|encryption]] designed to resist quantum attack.

**Searching and optimising.** Some problems, like finding the best routes for thousands of delivery trucks, might be helped, though by how much is still argued over.

[[@einstein|Albert Einstein]] was uneasy about entanglement. He called it "spooky action at a distance", because measuring one particle seemed to instantly affect another far away. Experiments since then have shown the effect is real. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to three scientists for experiments proving it. Entanglement can't be used to send messages faster than light, but quantum computers rely on it.

In 2019 Google said its 53-qubit chip, Sycamore, did a test calculation in about 200 seconds that would take the best supercomputer thousands of years. IBM argued a [[@supercomputers|supercomputer]] could do it in days. The task itself was useless, chosen only to show the machine's power.

Today's machines have hundreds or a few thousand qubits, but they make too many errors for most real work. Researchers are building error correction, which uses many physical qubits to make one reliable one. In 2023 India approved a National Quantum Mission of about ₹6,000 crore to build its own machines. Companies and labs in the United States, China and Europe are racing too. Nobody knows whether the winning qubit will be a cold circuit, a trapped atom or something not yet invented.

sec.t:
ताइनो लोगों ने अजनबियों का स्वागत किया और उनसे लेन-देन किया। कोलंबस ने लिखा कि ये अच्छे नौकर बनेंगे। इसी सोच ने आगे की घटनाओं की दिशा तय की।

हिस्पानियोला के गवर्नर के तौर पर उन्होंने ताइनो लोगों से ज़बरदस्ती सोना ढुँढवाया और उन्हें कड़ी सज़ाएँ दीं। कुछ को ग़ुलाम बनाकर स्पेन भेज दिया गया। यूरोप से आई [[@smallpox|चेचक]] जैसी बीमारियों ने, जिनका सामना इन लोगों ने पहले कभी नहीं किया था, बहुत बड़ी तादाद में जानें लीं। कुछ ही दशकों में हिस्पानियोला की ताइनो आबादी लगभग ख़त्म हो गई। स्पेन के शासक भी उनके राज से नाख़ुश हो गए, और 1500 में उन्हें गिरफ़्तार करके ज़ंजीरों में बाँधकर वापस भेजा गया।

कोलंबस की यात्राओं से वह सिलसिला शुरू हुआ जिसे इतिहासकार "कोलंबियन एक्सचेंज" कहते हैं। [[@corn-maize|मक्का]], [[@potatoes|आलू]], [[@tomatoes|टमाटर]] और [[@food-why-chillies-red|मिर्च]] अमेरिका से यूरोप, अफ़्रीका और एशिया पहुँचे। घोड़े, गायें, गेहूँ और गन्ना उल्टी दिशा में गए।

इसीलिए आज का भारतीय खाना अमेरिका के पौधों से भरा है। 1500 के दशक से पहले भारतीय सब्ज़ियों में न मिर्च थी, न समोसे में आलू। सोचो, बिना आलू के समोसा। [[@chillies|मिर्च]] शायद 1500 के दशक में पुर्तगाली व्यापारियों के साथ भारत आई।

इन महाद्वीपों का नाम एक दूसरे इतालवी, अमेरिगो वेस्पुची, के नाम पर पड़ा, जिन्होंने दलील दी कि यह एक "नई दुनिया" है। 1498 में पुर्तगाली [[expedition|खोजी]] वास्को दा गामा अफ़्रीका का चक्कर लगाकर असली भारत पहुँचे, और [[@kerala|केरल]] में कालीकट के पास उतरे।

अमेरिका में 1937 से पूरे देश में कोलंबस दिवस मनाया जाता है। बहुत से अमेरिकी, ख़ासकर इतालवी मूल के लोग, इसे हिम्मत और अपनी विरासत का जश्न मानते हैं। दूसरी ओर बहुत से लोग, जिनमें कई मूल अमेरिकी भी हैं, इसे क़ब्ज़े की शुरुआत का सम्मान मानते हैं। इसलिए कुछ राज्य और शहर अब इसकी जगह या इसके साथ-साथ [[indigenous|मूलनिवासी]] लोगों का दिवस मनाते हैं।

text: The Satavahanas were a [[dynasty|dynasty]] that ruled much of the Deccan plateau, in today's Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, for roughly 300 years. They rose after the [[@mauryan-empire|Mauryan Empire]] broke up, and were most powerful from about the 1st century BCE to the early 3rd century CE.

Their capital was Pratishthana, today's Paithan on the Godavari river, and later they moved east towards Amaravati. They grew rich from farming and from trade, including trade with the Roman world by sea. They also gave land and money to Buddhist monks, and some of India's oldest cave [[monastery|monasteries]] were carved in their time.

sec.t:
Many Satavahana kings were known by their mother's name. Gautamiputra Satakarni means "Satakarni, son of Gautami". His son was Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, "son of Vasishthi".

This does not mean women ruled, since the throne passed from father to son. Historians think it may show how important a mother's family was in Deccan society. Queens were certainly powerful. Gautamiputra's mother, Gautami Balashri, had a long [[inscription|inscription]] carved at the Buddhist caves near Nashik praising her son. An earlier queen, Naganika, recorded grand sacrifices made by her husband in an inscription at Naneghat, a mountain pass in the Western Ghats.

The Satavahanas controlled roads linking inland cities to ports on the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. A Greek sailors' guide from the 1st century CE, the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*, names Paithan and the busy port of Barygaza, today's Bharuch.

Traders sent [[@food-pepper-black-gold|pepper]], cotton cloth, beads and spices to the [[@ancient-rome|Roman Empire]]. Roman gold and silver coins, wine jars and pottery have been dug up across south India. Some Satavahana coins even show a two-masted ship, a sign that sea trade mattered to the kings. Their coins are mostly made of lead, copper and a mix called potin, small change for busy markets.

The Satavahana period saw Buddhist monks and merchants pay for magnificent rock-cut caves. The great prayer hall at Karla, near Lonavala, has a high curved ceiling and rows of carved pillars. The oldest caves at Ajanta, caves 9 and 10, date from around this time too. In the east, the great [[stupa|stupa]] at Amaravati was decorated with fine carved panels.

The kings wrote their inscriptions in Prakrit, an everyday language rather than Sanskrit. A collection of 700 short Prakrit love poems, the *Gatha Saptashati*, is traditionally credited to a Satavahana king called Hala. Some of its verses describe village life, rain and farm work in ways that still feel fresh.

By the early 3rd century CE the kingdom broke into smaller pieces ruled by local families, such as the Ikshvakus in Andhra. The [[@trade-routes|trade routes]] and Buddhist sites they protected lived on, and the Prakrit of their inscriptions is an ancestor of the Marathi spoken around Paithan today.

text: The Swadeshi movement was a protest that began in 1905, when the British government divided the province of Bengal into two. Swadeshi means "of one's own country". Its idea was to hit Britain where it hurt, in trade, by refusing British goods and buying Indian ones.

People burned foreign cloth, salt and sugar in public. Shops refused to sell British goods. Students left government schools. Indians started their own factories, banks, schools and shipping companies. Songs, poems and paintings spread the message. It was one of the first times the freedom struggle went beyond meetings and petitions to change what ordinary people bought and wore every day.

sec.t:
Boycotting was only half the plan. The other half was building. The chemist Prafulla Chandra Ray's company, Bengal Chemicals, grew quickly as people chose Indian medicines and soaps. Indian [[textile|textile]] mills and handloom weavers found new customers.

In 1906, V.O. Chidambaram Pillai, a lawyer in Tuticorin in Tamil Nadu, started the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company to run ships to Sri Lanka against a British firm. In 1907, Tata Iron and Steel raised its money from Indian investors in just a few weeks, in the Swadeshi spirit. A National Council of Education set up schools and colleges taught by Indians.

The movement had a soundtrack. Tagore wrote songs, including "Amar Sonar Bangla", which later became Bangladesh's national anthem. The painter Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata, showing India as a calm woman in saffron robes holding a book, rice, cloth and a rosary.

The movement spread well beyond Bengal. In Maharashtra, [[@tilak|Bal Gangadhar Tilak]] led bonfires of foreign cloth. In Punjab, Lala Lajpat Rai took up the call. In the south, crowds gathered to hear speakers in Tamil and Telugu.

Three leaders became so linked with the movement that people called them Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai from Punjab, Bal Gangadhar Tilak from Maharashtra and Bipin Chandra Pal from Bengal. They wanted bolder action than older Congress leaders, who preferred polite petitions. Since 2015, India has marked 7 August as National Handloom Day, remembering the day the boycott was declared.

By 1908 the movement had slowed. The British arrested leaders, including Tilak, who was sent to prison in Burma. Chidambaram Pillai was jailed too, and his company collapsed. The Congress split between moderates and those who wanted bolder action. Some young people, frustrated, turned to secret groups using violence.

Swadeshi also had weaknesses. Indian goods often cost more, which hurt poor families. Many Muslim peasants in eastern Bengal, who had gained from the new province, stayed away. Still, in 1911 the British reversed the partition. The idea of Swadeshi stayed alive, and Gandhi later made homespun [[@khadi|khadi]] its symbol across India.

text: Madhya Pradesh means "Central Province", and the name is a good description. The state sits in the very middle of India, with no coastline and borders with five other states. The Tropic of Cancer runs right across it. For decades, until Chhattisgarh was split off in 2000, it was India's biggest state by area. Today it's second, after Rajasthan.

It is "the heart of India" in other ways too. Its forests hold more wild tigers than any other state. Some of India's most famous ancient places are here: the painted rock shelters of [[@art-cave-paintings-bhimbetka|Bhimbetka]], the Buddhist stupas of Sanchi, and the carved temples of [[@khajuraho|Khajuraho]].

st.prompt: Most big Indian rivers flow east into the Bay of Bengal. Which way does Madhya Pradesh's Narmada flow?
st.reveal: The Narmada runs west through a long rift valley between two ranges of hills, the Vindhyas and the Satpuras. It reaches the Arabian Sea in Gujarat, which makes it one of very few big Indian rivers to flow west.

sec.t:
Near Bhopal, among forested hills, are the Bhimbetka rock shelters. They were discovered by an [[archaeologist|archaeologist]], V. S. Wakankar, who noticed the rocks from a train window in 1957. Inside, hundreds of overhanging rocks are covered with [[@cave-art|cave paintings]] in red and white.

They show hunters, dancers, horse riders, deer, [[@wild-indian-gaur|bison]] and elephants. Some are thought to be around 10,000 years old, and people kept painting here for thousands of years afterwards. UNESCO listed Bhimbetka as a World Heritage Site in 2003.

At Sanchi, the emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] built a great [[stupa|stupa]], a dome-shaped Buddhist monument, in the 3rd century BCE. Later rulers enlarged it and added four beautifully carved stone gateways covered with stories of the Buddha's life. Strangely, the Buddha himself isn't shown as a person in these carvings. He is represented by symbols, such as a tree, a wheel or footprints.

Khajuraho, in the north of the state, has temples built about a thousand years ago by the Chandela kings. Their walls are covered with thousands of carved figures of gods, musicians, dancers and animals. Only a couple of dozen of the original temples survive, out of many more. Because they stood in quiet countryside, far from big cities, they escaped much of the damage that hit other temples, and they became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

The Narmada river begins at Amarkantak and flows west through a valley between two ranges of hills. At Bhedaghat, near Jabalpur, it cuts through gleaming white marble rocks. Many Hindus consider the Narmada sacred, and some pilgrims walk all the way along both banks, a journey of thousands of kilometres.

The state is home to many Adivasi communities, including the Gond and the Bhil. [[@gond-art|Gond art]], with its animals and trees made of dots and fine lines, has travelled from village walls to galleries around the world. Painters like Jangarh Singh Shyam helped make it famous, and his style lives on in a new generation of Gond artists.

text: After 1994, when South Africa held its first election in which people of every race could vote, Archbishop Desmond Tutu began calling it the "Rainbow Nation". [[@apartheid|Nelson Mandela]], the new president, used the phrase too.

The idea was simple. A rainbow has many colours, and it is beautiful because they sit side by side. South Africa has people whose families are Black African, white, Indian and of mixed heritage, speaking a dozen official languages. The nickname was a hope that all of them could share one country after decades of being kept apart by law.

st.prompt: Most countries have one capital city. How many does South Africa have?
st.reveal: Pretoria is where the president and government offices work. Cape Town is home to parliament, and Bloemfontein to the Supreme Court of Appeal. The split was a compromise made when the country was formed in 1910.

The real southern tip is Cape Agulhas, about 150 km to the south-east. Cape Agulhas is also where geographers draw the line between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

sec.t:
In 1893 a young lawyer named [[@gandhi-south-africa|Mohandas Gandhi]] arrived in South Africa to work on a court case. That year he was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for sitting in a carriage reserved for white passengers. He stayed for over twenty years, and it was here that he first organised peaceful mass protest. You can follow what happened next in the story of [[@gandhi|Gandhi]].

Today about one and a half million South Africans have Indian roots, many of them in and around Durban. Their families mostly arrived in the late 1800s to work on sugar plantations. Durban's bunny chow, a hollowed-out loaf filled with curry, grew from that mix.

South Africa has twelve official languages. They include isiZulu, isiXhosa, Afrikaans, English, Sesotho and Setswana. In 2023, South African [[@sign-language|Sign Language]] became the twelfth. The national anthem itself switches between five languages in a single song.

Many South Africans switch languages every day: one at home, another at school, a third with friends. That is ordinary in India too, where plenty of children speak two or three languages before they learn to read. You can see how common this is in the article on [[@languages-world|languages around the world]].

The land is as mixed as the people. [[@world-cape-town|Cape Town]] sits beneath Table Mountain, whose flat top is often covered by a white sheet of cloud locals call the "tablecloth". To the north-east, Kruger National Park is one of Africa's largest wildlife reserves, home to lions, elephants and rhinos.

South Africa's coast touches two oceans. The cold Atlantic washes the west, and the warm Indian Ocean the east. The water on a beach near Durban can feel bath-warm, while Cape Town's is chilly enough to make you gasp.

The cold western current brings up food from the deep, so the sea there is full of fish, seals and seabirds. Near Cape Town, a colony of African [[@penguin-flight|penguins]] waddles across a public beach called Boulders, a few minutes' walk from people's houses. [[@ocean-penguins-swim|Penguins]] on an African beach sound odd, but the chilly water suits them. Out at sea, great white sharks hunt the seals, and in the warmer east, whales pass close enough to shore to be watched from cliff tops.

text: The ancient Greeks worshipped many gods. The most important were the twelve Olympians, who were said to live on Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece. Zeus, god of the sky and [[@thunder-sound|thunder]], was their king. His brother Poseidon ruled the sea, and another brother, Hades, ruled the land of the dead.

The Greeks told stories, called myths, about these gods and about heroes like Heracles and Odysseus. The myths explained storms, seasons and stars, and taught what people thought was brave or foolish. For more than a thousand years, the gods were part of everyday religion in Greek temples, homes and festivals.

st.prompt: One of these English words comes from the name of a Greek god. Which one?
st.reveal: Pan was the goat-legged god of wild places and shepherds. The Greeks said his sudden shouts could fill people with terror, and that fear was called "panic". Echo, atlas and museum also come from Greek myths.

The poet Hesiod describes a pithos, a big storage jar. In the 1500s the scholar Erasmus mistranslated it as a box, and the box stuck.

sec.t:
The Greek gods were powerful but far from perfect. They fell in love, held grudges, played favourites and fought among themselves. Zeus's wife Hera was queen of the gods and protector of marriage, and she was often furious with her husband.

Athena, goddess of wisdom and craft, was said to have sprung fully grown from Zeus's head. The city of Athens took her name, and its great temple, the Parthenon, was built for her. Apollo was god of music, light and prophecy. His twin Artemis ruled hunting and the Moon. Hermes, with winged sandals, carried messages. Hephaestus worked a forge, and Aphrodite was goddess of love.

In one story, a weaver called Arachne boasted that she was better than Athena. She lost the contest that followed, and Athena turned her into a spider. That is why spiders, scorpions and their relatives belong to a group called arachnids. Scientists still use names from Greek myths for new [[species|species]] and space missions.

The [[@olympics|Olympic Games]] began at Olympia, a [[sanctuary|sanctuary]] of Zeus, and the traditional start date is 776 BCE. When the Romans conquered Greece, they matched the Greek gods with their own. Zeus became [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]], Aphrodite became Venus and Ares became Mars. Those Roman names now belong to [[@planets-size|the planets]].

You can find the myths in the [[@constellations|night sky]], where Orion, Perseus and Andromeda have their own star patterns. They live on in words like echo, atlas and museum, which once meant a home of the Muses. A sportswear brand is named after Nike, the winged goddess of victory.

Few people worship the Olympians today, but the stories keep finding new readers. Rick Riordan's [[@percy-jackson|Percy Jackson]] books, first published in 2005, follow the gods' children at an American summer camp. Indian readers often compare Homer's epics with the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], which also have great wars, long journeys and gods who take sides.

The ruins of [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]] still stand in Athens, Delphi and Olympia. Visitors walk where pilgrims once came to ask Apollo's oracle about the future. His answers were famous for being so puzzling that people could read them more than one way.

text: Flood stories appear in Mesopotamia, India, Greece, China, the Americas, Australia and elsewhere. In many, a god or wise being warns one good person, who builds a boat or finds a high place, survives with family and animals, and starts the world again.

Scholars think there are several reasons. People almost everywhere lived beside rivers and coasts, where terrible [[@floods-why|floods]] really happened. At the end of the last ice age, rising seas drowned land that people knew. And some stories travelled from one people to another, changing as they went. Each culture also used the story to say something about gods, goodness and new beginnings.

st.prompt: In the Indian flood story, who warns Manu that a great flood is coming?

options.t: A small fish he saves, who turns out to be Vishnu

st.reveal: Manu rescues a little fish, which grows enormous and warns him of the flood. It tows his boat to safety with a rope tied to its horn. In later texts, the fish is Matsya, the first avatar of Vishnu.

sec.t:
The earliest written flood stories come from [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], in what is now Iraq, about 4,000 years ago. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, a man named Utnapishtim is warned by the god Ea, who whispers through the reed wall of his house. He builds a huge boat, loads his family and animals, and survives a storm of six days and seven nights. Then he sends out birds to look for land.

In 1872, a self-taught scholar named George Smith, working at the British Museum, read this tablet for the first time in thousands of years. It caused a sensation, because it was so similar to the story of Noah in the Bible.

In [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]], Zeus floods the world, and Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survive in a chest that floats to a mountain. Afterwards, they throw stones over their shoulders, and the stones become new people.

China's story is different. Floods along the Yellow River last for years. A hero named Yu the Great tames them without any boat, by digging channels to lead the water to the sea. He works so hard that he passes his own house three times without going in. The Yellow River really has flooded catastrophically again and again in Chinese history.

About 20,000 years ago, at the height of the last [[@ice-ages|ice age]], sea level was about 120 m lower than today. As the ice melted, coasts moved inland, sometimes by many kilometres. Land bridges disappeared. People living on low coasts would have watched the sea creep closer over generations.

In 2016, two researchers studied 21 Aboriginal stories from around Australia's coast describing the sea drowning land. Matching them with sea-level records, they argued some may preserve memories more than 7,000 years old, passed down by word of mouth. Not everyone agrees, but it shows how long a story can survive.

For Jews, Christians and Muslims, the story of Noah (Nuh in the Quran) carries religious meaning, and for Hindus the story of Manu and Matsya does too. People read them as faith, history, lessons or all three.

Floods are not just stories of the past. Today, [[@sea-level-rise|sea level]] is rising again by a few millimetres every year, and low-lying places from the Sundarbans to Miami are planning for higher water.

text: There is no official list, and every family has its own favourites. But some poems keep turning up in homes and classrooms in India and America, because they are fun to say and easy to remember. A few are silly, a few are brave, and a few are quietly beautiful.
Here are some worth knowing, why they last, and the people who wrote them. Many of them are short enough to learn in a week.

st.prompt: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star is sung to a tune that is also used for which other song?
st.reveal: The tune is an old French melody. It carries Twinkle, Twinkle, the ABC song and Baa, Baa, Black Sheep, which is one reason so many children learn all three together.

myth: Ring a Ring o' Roses is secretly about the plague.

Experts on nursery rhymes have found no evidence for this. The rhyme was first printed in the 1880s, centuries after the great plague, and the plague story only became popular in the twentieth century.
