sec.t:
Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star began life as a poem called "The Star" by Jane Taylor, published in England in 1806. It is sung to an old French tune that also carries the ABC song. Most people only know the first verse, but there are five.

Nursery rhymes like this last because of [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]]. A strong beat and rhyming words act like hooks for your [[@memory|memory]], which is why you can still sing rhymes you learned before you could read.

Every Indian language has its own first rhymes. Many Hindi-speaking toddlers learn "Machli jal ki rani hai", about a fish who is queen of the water and dies if taken out of it. In Tamil Nadu, small children hear "Nila nila odi vaa", which begs the Moon to come running down to play. Nobody is sure who first made up most of these. They passed from parent to child long before anyone printed them.

In 1871 Edward Lear wrote "The Owl and the Pussy-cat", about an owl and a cat who sail away "in a beautiful pea-green boat" and eat with a runcible spoon. Nobody knows exactly what a runcible spoon is, because Lear invented the word.

Bengal has its own king of nonsense. [[@sukumar-ray|Sukumar Ray]] filled his 1923 book *Abol Tabol* with strange creatures, such as a duck crossed with a porcupine. Children still recite it in Kolkata, and his son, the film director Satyajit Ray, grew up surrounded by it. In America, Dr. Seuss and Shel Silverstein carried the same spirit. Silverstein's *Where the Sidewalk Ends* (1974) is full of poems about kids who refuse to take out the rubbish.

[[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]] wrote "Where the mind is without fear" as part of *Gitanjali*, the collection that helped him win the Nobel Prize in 1913. It describes a country where knowledge is free and people are not divided by narrow walls. Many Indian schools use it in assemblies.

Robert Frost's "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening" (1923) is about a rider pausing to watch snow fall in a dark wood. It ends by repeating one line, "And miles to go before I sleep". That simple repeat is why so many people remember it.

The best poem for you might not be on anyone's list. Try a library, a poetry app or a grandparent who knows old songs in Tamil, Marathi or Spanish. Read poems aloud, because poetry was spoken long before it was written down. If two lines stay in your head all day, you've found one worth keeping.

text: Jackfruit is a huge, green, bumpy fruit that grows on a tall evergreen tree. It is the largest fruit that grows on trees anywhere. Many weigh 5 to 20 kilograms, and the biggest have topped 50 kilograms, about as much as a sack of rice. Because they are so heavy, they grow directly from the trunk and the thickest branches.

Inside the spiky skin are hundreds of yellow, sweet pods, each wrapped around a large seed. Ripe jackfruit tastes a bit like banana, mango and pineapple mixed together. Unripe jackfruit is cooked as a vegetable, and the seeds are roasted or added to curries.

st.prompt: Where on the tree does a jackfruit grow?

options.t: Straight out of the trunk and thick branches
At the very tips of thin branches

st.reveal: Jackfruits sprout from short stalks on the trunk and the thickest branches. Thin twigs could never hold a fruit that may weigh as much as a child. Some old trees even grow fruit near their roots.

myth: Young jackfruit is a meat replacement that is full of protein like chicken.
Cooked unripe jackfruit can feel stringy and chewy like pulled meat, which is why it is popular in vegan dishes. But it has very little protein. Its seeds have more, and beans and dal have much more.

sec.t:
Cutting a jackfruit is messy. The fruit is full of a sticky white sap, a kind of latex, that clings to knives and hands like glue. Cooks rub oil on their hands and blades first, and spread newspaper on the floor. Usually an adult cuts the fruit into big wedges, and then the family pulls out the pods together.

Jackfruit has a strong smell when it is ripe, sweet and a bit like overripe banana. Some people love it and some can't stand it. It is often confused with durian, a Southeast Asian fruit that smells far stronger, but the two are not related.

In Kerala and Karnataka, jackfruit season brings chips, jams, sweet halwa, payasam and steamed cakes wrapped in leaves. Raw jackfruit is cooked in spicy dishes. In Bengal it is made into a curry so meaty in texture that it is sometimes called "tree mutton".

Unripe jackfruit has become popular in Britain and the USA as a [[@vegetarian|vegetarian]] swap for pulled pork in burgers and tacos. The tree's golden-brown wood is strong and doesn't warp easily. Carpenters use it for furniture, and instrument makers use it for the body of the [[@veena|veena]].

In Sri Lanka, the jackfruit tree is sometimes called "bath gasa", meaning rice tree, because its fruit has helped feed families when rice was short. A big jackfruit can be cooked like a vegetable while young, eaten as a sweet fruit when ripe, and its seeds kept for later.

Those seeds are worth saving. Roasted or boiled, they taste a little like chestnuts, and they can be ground into flour for rotis and cakes. In South India the main season runs roughly from March to July, and in good years there is so much fruit that some of it goes to waste. Food scientists and small companies are now drying, freezing and packing jackfruit so it can be eaten all year.

Jackfruit belongs to the same plant family as figs, mulberries and the [[@banyan|banyan]]. That is why it has sticky sap like a fig. What looks like one fruit is really hundreds of tiny flowers that have fused together, with each yellow pod grown from a single flower.

One tree can produce more than 100 fruits a year. Because the trees are tough and need little care, scientists see jackfruit as a useful food for a warming world. In many villages, a single old jackfruit tree feeds a family and their neighbours all season.

text: A silkworm is not a worm. It is the caterpillar of a moth called Bombyx mori. It spends about a month eating mulberry leaves and growing. Then it spins a [[cocoon|cocoon]] around itself, where it will change into a moth.

The cocoon is made from one long, unbroken thread of silk, a [[protein|protein]] the caterpillar squeezes out from [[gland|glands]] near its mouth. Silk farmers soften the cocoons in hot water and carefully unwind that thread. Several threads are twisted together to make yarn, which is then woven into shining cloth.

st.prompt: A silkworm will only eat one kind of food. What is it?
st.reveal: Domestic silkworms feed almost entirely on mulberry leaves, and they eat a lot. A silkworm grows thousands of times heavier in about a month. That is why silk farmers in Karnataka and elsewhere grow fields of mulberry bushes.

myth: Silkworms are worms.
Silkworms are caterpillars, the young stage of a moth. If left alone, a silkworm turns into a pale, furry moth inside its cocoon. Domesticated silk moths cannot fly.

sec.t:
A silkworm hatches from an egg smaller than a pinhead. For about four weeks it does almost nothing but eat mulberry leaves, shedding its skin four times as it grows.

When it is ready, it begins to spin. Moving its head in a figure-of-eight, it pushes out two strands of silk glued together with a gum called sericin. Over two or three days it wraps itself in a cocoon about the size of a peanut. A single cocoon's thread is often several hundred metres long, and sometimes much more.

If the caterpillar were left alone, it would become a moth and break out of the cocoon, cutting the long thread into short pieces. So most silk farmers steam or boil the cocoons first, which kills the [[pupa|pupa]] inside.

The hot water also softens the gum, so workers can find the end of the thread and reel it off. Several threads are wound together to make one strand of raw silk. Because many silkworms die in this process, some people choose [[ahimsa|ahimsa]] silk, made after the moths have escaped.

India is the world's second-largest silk producer, after China. Most is mulberry silk, and Karnataka grows the most, which is why Mysore silk is famous. But India also makes three kinds of wild or semi-wild silk.

Tasar silk comes from moths that feed on trees like arjun and sal in Jharkhand and nearby states. Eri silk, from Assam, comes from caterpillars that eat castor leaves. Muga silk, with its natural golden shine, is made almost entirely in Assam in [[@northeast-india|Northeast India]].

Silk is woven into some of India's most loved cloth. Kanchipuram [[@weaving-saree|sarees]] from Tamil Nadu are heavy silks with bright borders. Banarasi sarees from [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] are woven with gold and silver threads. Many families save silk sarees for weddings and festivals, and pass them down for generations.

Silkworms are not the only animals that spin silk. Spiders make several kinds from glands on their bodies, and some insects use silk for nests. Scientists study these threads because they are strong, light and stretchy. Some labs are even trying to make artificial silk from proteins grown by [[microbe|microbes]].
